conflicts.point: Whether compute-based regulatory thresholds can maintain stable exemptions for smaller developers or whether they are inevitably subject to downward lobbying pressure by incumbents.

positions.stance: Tying verification requirements strictly to systemic compute thresholds, such as $10^{26}$ training FLOPs, protects smaller developers and open-source teams from regulatory capture while addressing frontier risks.
Compute thresholds establish an arbitrary moving target that dominant firms will weaponize and lobby to lower over time, turning exemptions into permanent barriers to market entry.

conflicts.point: Whether distributed open-source scrutiny provides superior structural security compared to centralized regulatory pre-deployment verification.

positions.stance: Decentralized open-source codebases and public peer-review deliver superior structural safety and rapid innovation compared to closed administrative licensing silos.
Complex frontier systems require mandatory ex-ante verification gates and outside technical audits to prevent catastrophic, irreversible failures prior to deployment.

verdicts.conflict: Whether compute-based regulatory thresholds can maintain stable exemptions for smaller developers or whether they are subject to downward lobbying pressure.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions rely on plausible institutional dynamics regarding regulatory capture and cost burdens without definitive historical proof from the frontier AI sector. The safetyist argument correctly identifies compute thresholds as a logical technical filter, but the accelerationist critique correctly notes that regulatory thresholds are frequent targets for rent-seeking behavior over time. Longitudinal data on how tech incumbents lobby regulatory bodies regarding computational floors is required to tip the balance.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical evidence showing that compute thresholds either successfully preserve open-source ecosystems over multiple legislative cycles or invariably get ratcheted downward by incumbent lobbying.

verdicts.conflict: Whether distributed open-source scrutiny provides superior structural security compared to centralized regulatory pre-deployment verification.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist and accelerationist positions prioritize competing risk vectors without a common empirical benchmark for safety outcomes. Decentralized peer review offers broad participation and rapid innovation, but fails to provide ex-ante guarantees against catastrophic misuses of highly scalable models. Conversely, centralized verification reduces systemic deployment risks but introduces single points of regulatory failure and market gatekeeping.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Comparative incident data demonstrating whether ex-ante centralized audits or decentralized open-source post-deployment monitoring prevent more severe model safety failures.
